paras: The killing of Jennie McCall was the shooting death of a Black woman by a mob at her house near Jennings, Florida, on the night of Tuesday, October 27, 1903. The mob had come for her husband and, believing he was inside, fired a volley into the house. An Associated Press dispatch from Jacksonville carried the story to papers from Maine to Mississippi, and the St. Paul Appeal, a Black newspaper, reprinted a Chicago account in which she died defending her husband.

According to the Associated Press dispatch, dated Jacksonville, October 28, a "mob of men" went to the McCall house near Jennings the night before in an attempt "to secure her husband." The mob surrounded the house and, "thinking he was inside, fired a volley into the house, instantly killing the woman." The dispatch gave neither the husband's first name nor any reason for the mob's pursuit of him.

A fuller version, sent as a special dispatch to the Chicago Inter Ocean and reprinted in the St. Paul Appeal, said the mob demanded the husband's surrender after surrounding the house. In that account Jennie McCall had barricaded the doors and windows and told the men, "You must kill me before you harm him." "A volley of shots answered her," the report continued, "and she fell dead, her body riddled with bullets."

The first dispatch said that a posse was "said to be in pursuit of the assailants," and other printings reported the same pursuit. No report of an arrest, an inquest or a trial, and no later news of the husband, was found in the coverage.

Most of the coverage was a three-sentence Associated Press item that ran on October 29 in the Savannah Morning News, the Raleigh News & Observer, the Montgomery Advertiser, the St. Paul Globe, the Washington Evening Star and the Daily Kennebec Journal of Augusta, Maine. The Washington Times and the Birmingham Age-Herald carried it the next day under later datelines, and small papers in North Carolina and Mississippi reprinted it as late as November 7, still saying "last night" or "Tuesday night." Several printings shortened it to a single sentence, and the Monroe Journal dropped the posse.

White headlines dwelt on the mob's error: the Savannah Morning News used "Killed a Woman" over the deck "Florida Mob Was After Her Husband But She Was Its Victim," and the News & Observer used "Killed the Wife Instead of Husband." Others ran "Woman Killed By Mob," "Mob Slays a Woman" and, in the St. Paul Globe, "Dies for Her Husband," over a text that called her "a negress." The wire text named her as "a negro woman," left the mob undescribed and carried no comment.

The St. Paul Appeal printed the story on its front page on November 7 under the headline "MOB MURDERS WOMAN" and the deck "Angry Crowd at Jacksonville, Fla., Shoots Wife of Man Whose Life Is Sought." The item appeared on a page that opened with a compilation of "INFAMOUS CRIMES" by the "WHITE RACE," beside reports of assaults on girls in St. Paul and Chicago. Where the white papers stressed that the mob killed the wrong person, the Appeal's version called the act murder and presented Jennie McCall as dying in her husband's defense.

The printings of the wire sentence disagree on who was attempting what: most say the mob was trying "to secure" the husband, the Washington Times says "seize" and the Evening Star "arrest." Others make the wife the actor, trying to "shelter," "secrete" or "save" him, a reading closer to the Inter Ocean account of her trying "to save her husband from the fury of a mob." The Appeal's headline also placed the shooting "at Jacksonville," the city where both dispatches were filed, while the Associated Press text put the house near Jennings.

reader.title: Killing of Jennie McCall
bases: A mob of men hunting her husband surrounded the McCall house near Jennings, Fla., and fired a volley into it, killing Jennie McCall (A1, A14).

A 'mob of men' with no stated authority besieged a Black family's house and shot the woman dead, and a posse was sent after them as 'assailants' (A1, A8); the mob was hunting her husband, whose life it 'sought' (A14), but no report states what he was accused of, so the pretext is not shown.

The Associated Press dispatch (A1 and its printings A2-A13) and a separate special dispatch to the Chicago Inter Ocean reprinted by the St. Paul Appeal (A14) agree on the core event, though both came from Jacksonville and no local Florida report was found.

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch from Jacksonville
accounts.gist: While trying to 'secure' her husband, a mob surrounded the house near Jennings, fired a volley believing he was inside, and killed Jennie McCall instantly; a posse was said to be in pursuit.

accounts.label: Special to the Chicago Inter Ocean, reprinted by the St. Paul Appeal
accounts.gist: The mob demanded her husband's surrender; she had barricaded doors and windows and told the mob, 'You must kill me before you harm him,' and was answered with a volley that riddled her body.

framing.detail: Brief AP item under headlines such as 'Killed a Woman' with the deck 'Florida Mob Was After Her Husband But She Was Its Victim,' 'Mob Slays a Woman' and 'Dies for Her Husband,' with no editorial comment.
The Appeal headed the story 'MOB MURDERS WOMAN,' printed her defiance of the mob, and ran it on a front page that opened with a compilation of crimes by the 'white race.'

versions.value: 'attempting to save her husband'; 'to save her husband from the fury of a mob'

conflicts.note: All white versions are the same AP sentence; the verb changed between printings, so that some make the mob the actor and others the wife. The Inter Ocean account (A14) supports the reading that she was trying to save him.
Jacksonville is the dateline of both dispatches; the AP text places the house near Jennings, and the Appeal's own body text names no town.

conflicts.field: date of printing vs. date of event

versions.value: 'last night' in a dispatch dated Oct. 28 (i.e. Oct. 27); 'Tuesday night'

conflicts.note: The Oct. 28 dispatch and the 'Tuesday night' wording fix the shooting at the night of Oct. 27; the later datelines are re-dated printings of the same text.

record_check.dossier: 1903-10-27 (night of Tuesday; 'last night' in a dispatch dated Oct. 28). Nov. 3-7 dates are late reprints.
No county is named in the coverage; papers say only 'near Jennings, Fla.'
1903-10-27 is the only date the texts support
At least 11 white printings from 1903-10-29 to 1903-11-07, and one Black-press report (St. Paul Appeal, 1903-11-07)

record_check.record: A posse was reported in pursuit of the assailants
record_check.dossier: Supported; add that the mob believed the husband was inside and that the Black-press version has her defying the mob
